items.title: I Tried this Trending Opensource Claude Code Plugin & IT'S ACTUALLY CRAZY!
items.summary:
Cline Desktop: https://cline.gg/desktop-aick
ClinePass: https://cline.gg/clinepass-aick
PandaCode: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode
Join this channel to get access to perks: https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I'll take a look at Claude-Mem, an open-source memory system that gives Claude Code and other coding agents memory across sessions. I'll show how it works with lifecycle hooks, a local worker and an observer model, and how its progressive disclosure index keeps the start of a new session small. Then I'll install it with the Claude provider, have Claude fix a time zone bug, and test whether a completely fresh session remembers the fix, plus the new My Work page. After that, I'll get into the privacy problem with the browser setup that uploaded the last 30 days of prompts to cmem.ai without asking until version 15.8.3, along with telemetry, redaction and the cost, and finally whether you should actually use it.
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So, the most annoying thing about Claude code is not the rate limits. It's that every new session starts with amnesia. You spend an hour fixing a bug with it, you explain why you made a decision, you close the terminal, and the next morning it knows nothing. So, you explain it all over again, and it reads the same files all over again, and you pay for those tokens all over again. Now, there's a project called Claude Mem that tries to fix this. It has more than 112,000 stars on GitHub, close to 10,000 forks. It's under Apache 2, and version 15.9 came out just 2 days ago. So, this is not some small experiment anymore. But there's also a privacy issue that you need to know about before you install it, and I'll get to that as well. So, let's get right into it. Claude Mem is a a memory system for coding agents. It watches what your agent does during a session, compresses that into short notes, and then gives the relevant notes back to the agent in future sessions. You don't have to call anything or remember any command. It just runs in the background. Now, it's worth understanding how this works because it's pretty clever. It uses Claude code's lifecycle hooks. There are hooks for when a session starts, when you submit a prompt before and after every tool call, when Claude stops, and when the session ends. So, every time Claude reads a file, edits something, or runs a command, Claude Mem sees it. Those events go to a small worker service that runs locally on your machine. The worker hands them to an observer, which is just another model running in the background on the Claude provider. That's Haiku. The observer turns the raw tool calls into what they call observations. An observation has a title, a type like bug fix or decision, a short narrative, some facts, and the files involved. Then all of it goes into a SQLite database on your machine with a Chroma vector database next to it for search by meaning. And when a session ends, you also get a summary of what you asked for, what was investigated, what was learned, and what the next steps are. So, that's the writing side. The reading side is where the idea really is. The obvious to build memory is to dump all your history into the context. That's terrible because you burn thousands of tokens on stuff that isn't relevant. So Claude Mem does something called progressive disclosure. When a new session starts, it injects an index of your recent observations. By default, that's the last 50. It's only the titles and the types along with how many tokens it would cost to read them. So the agent sees what exists and it decides what is worth opening. Then if it needs more, it has three search tools. First is search, which returns a compact list of IDs at around 50 to 100 tokens per result only for the IDs that it picked. They claim about 10 times the token savings from filtering before fetching. Take that with a grain of salt though because their own website says that the effect on token use depends on your workload and your provider, which is a fair thing to say to be honest. Now let's install it. You just run npx Claude Mem install. Don't use npm install -g because that only installs the library and it doesn't set up the hooks or the worker. The installer sets up the runtime first and that includes Bun and UV if you don't have them. Then it wants you to sign in and pick a memory provider and their hosted one called CMAM Pro is pre-selected. You get a 30-day free trial on that, but you don't have to do any of that. If you pass the dash-dash provider flag with Claude, it skips the sign-in and memory just runs on your own Anthropic plan. You can also use your own Open Router or Gemini Key or any OpenAI compatible endpoint. So I'm going with the Claude provider here. Once that's done, I have a small invoice API and I'll start Claude code in it. There's a bug where an invoice due at the end of the month shows up a day early for some customers. So I'll ask Claude to find it and fix it. Let's send it and see. It looks around, reads the date code, and finds the issue. The due date is being parsed as local time, so the day shifts depending on the time zone. It changes that to UTC and it runs the tests and they pass. Now while this was happening, Claude Mem was recording all of it. If you open the worker URL in the browser, you can see the viewer. Here's the memory timeline and here are the observations that it just created. There's the bug fix with its title and its facts and the files that it touched. And there's the session summary with what was learned and what the next steps are. So now let's do the actual test. I'll close this session and start a completely fresh one. And if we look at the start of the session, there's the injected context. Here's the timeline of what happened with the types and the total cost to read it, which is just 425 tokens for these three observations. So that's the index I was talking about and it's pretty small. Now I'll ask it to add a reminder email that goes out three days before an invoice is due. I haven't told it anything about the date bug, but if you look at what it does, it already knows that due dates are handled in UTC. So it uses the same helper instead of writing its own date logic. That's exactly the kind of mistake that a fresh session would make. So this is kind of great. Let's try one more thing. I'll ask why did we change how due dates are parsed? Now it has no reason to dig through the code for this. It calls search and gets the smallest of IDs. Then it picks the right one and calls get observations and it answers with the actual reason, the time zone issue from the earlier session. I didn't have to explain anything, which is just amazing. There's also a newer page called my work and it's now the default page at that same local URL. It takes your recorded requests and shows what's being worked on, what's waiting on you, and what's done but not checked. You can press mark checked once you've reviewed something and that review stays local. If you run a lot of agents at once, this is actually pretty useful. And if you want the old memory timeline, it's still there under the classic viewer link. It also isn't just for Claude code anymore, despite the name. The dash dash ID flag supports Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Windsurf, Copilot, Kimi, Devin, Hermes, PI, the DeepSeek Coder and more. Version 15.9 just added Devin. There are also settings for writing the memories in around 30 languages and a chill mode that records fewer observations and keeps only what would be painful to rediscover. Now let's talk about the things that you should actually be careful about because this is where I have some problems with it. Here's the big one. In version 15.2, they added a browser setup step, and until a few days ago, that setup scanned your local history from Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, and others, and it uploaded the full text of your last 30 days of prompts to cmem.ai along with project names, folder paths, and timestamps. It did this as soon as the page loaded without asking. A user reported it in an issue, and according to that report, cmem.ai confirmed that the prompts went through Open Router without blocking providers that may keep or train on them. And this is while the privacy policy said that nothing leaves your device unless you turn on Cloud Sync. That's really bad to be honest. Now, it did get fixed. Version 15.8.3 from November 2nd stops and asks you first with a clear keep everything local option. So if you install it today, make sure that you're on 15.8.3 or later. But the release notes also say that prompts which were already uploaded are not removed by the update. So if you installed an earlier version with the browser setup, that's worth knowing. Telemetry is also on by default. It's anonymous and it's documented, and the installer does ask you once, but it's opt out. You can run npx cloud mem telemetry disable, and that's it. You can also set the do not track variable. The privacy tools themselves are decent. You can wrap anything in private tags, and that text won't be stored even though Claude can still use it in that session. There's also an auto redaction feature with 30 built-in patterns for things like API keys, but that one is opt in, and I think it should be on by default. So I turn it on with the redact enabled setting on day one. Then there's the cost. The engine is free and open source, but the observer is still a model doing work. On the Claude provider, memory shares your plan's usage, so it comes out of the same limits that you're already hitting. And there's an open issue where a user on the Claude provider saw around 230 hidden Codex runs in 4 days from the my work refresh, which used up their Codex quota. If you go with the hosted option, it's $30 a month after the trial, and then there's heavy at $70 and max at $100. And there's a file read gate that's on by default as well, which can block Claude from reading a large file that already has history and sends it to an outline instead. It usually saves tokens, but if Claude acts weird around big files, that's where to look. So, should you use it? If you work on the same project for weeks and you keep re-explaining the same decisions, then I think it's really useful. The idea is right, and the index approach is the smart way of doing this. If you only do small one-off tasks, you don't need it, and a good cloud.md file will do most of the work for free. If you do install it, use the dash dash provider flag, say no to the upload, disable telemetry, and turn on redaction. That's about 2 minutes of setup, and then you get the good part without the parts that I don't like. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video [music] a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music]

In this video, I'll show you billion-context, a small proxy that sits between your AI coding agent and the model API and lets the model compress its own history. I'll go over how its four tools work, what the author's paper and the third-party benchmarks on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash actually say, and the three ways to install it. Then I'll show how I would set it up with Cline and ClinePass through the OpenAI Compatible base URL, and where Cline Desktop and PandaCode fit in. I'll also cover the limitations, so you know what you are getting before you install it.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Billion-context is a proxy between your agent and the model API, and it aims at month-long single sessions and billions of tokens through one context window.
🧠 It gives the model four
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. So, if you use AI coding agents for long tasks, you know the problem. The session keeps growing, the context window fills up, and then the agent either compacts everything into one blurry summary or it just falls apart, and every single turn resends that whole history, so you're paying for the same tokens again and again. Now, there is a project on GitHub called Billion Context that is trying to fix this, and it has blown up. It is at about 3,700 stars and 300 forks in under 3 months. The pitch is month-long single sessions, billions of tokens through one context window, a 100k window being enough, and five times fewer tokens. So, in this video I want to show you what it actually does, what the benchmarks say, and how I set it up with Klein and Klein Pass so you get cheap open models and a session that does not die. I'll also show where Pandacode fits in. So, let's get right into it. Now, Billion Context is a small proxy. It sits between your agent and the model API. You point your agent's base URL at the proxy and every request goes through it. The proxy reads the conversation, compresses the parts that are already done, and then forwards it to the real model. It works with Anthropic and OpenAI style APIs, so it works with almost any agent. But the interesting part is how it compresses. It does not just cut the history off at some limit. Instead, it gives the model four new tools. Compress folds a range of messages into a detailed summary. Decompress brings a range back when the exact details are needed again. Search context does a keyword search over everything that was compressed, and ACP status shows how full the context is and what can still be compressed. So, the model itself decides when to compress and what to compress. And this is why it is different from the summarizer that is built into your agent. The compression is incremental, so it summarizes small ranges instead of the whole thing at once. It is reversible because anything can be decompressed and it keeps the prompt cache intact. They say healthy session sits at a 95 to 97% cash hit rate, and the compression itself costs 2% or less. That matters a lot because cash tokens are extremely cheap. Now let's talk about the numbers. The author has a paper in the repo and it covers 4 and 1/2 months of real use, 174,000 model calls and 18.76 billion input tokens with zero context window overflows on 200k models. There is also a third-party benchmark and it was run on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which is very relevant for this video on Context Bench, which is a coding agent exploring real repos. Billion context came first with an F1 of 0.31 ahead of the full context at 0.29 and it cost $4.61 instead of $11.05. So that is 58% cheaper and slightly better. On Long Mem of Al, it scored 79.2% against 83.2 for the full context and 62.6 for the best rag setup at 71% lower cost. And on a 1.48 million token test, the full context failed 199 out of 199 times while billion context survived every time with about 30 times compression. But it is not magic. On the needle in a haystack test where you need one exact sentence back, it dropped from 69% to 27%. So the summaries keep the meaning, not every exact word. For coding agents, that is usually the right trade, but you should know about it. Now let's set it up. You install it with npm install -g billion context with dash dash prefix set to your local folder and that gives you a command called Billy. Then there are three ways to use it. You can run Billy plugin install with the name of your client and it becomes a native plugin for clients like Pi, Open Code, Kimi Code, and Hermes. You can run Billy followed by the client name like Billy Claude or Billy Codex and it launches the client through the proxy without touching your config. Or for anything else, you just start Billy and put the proxy address in front of your base URL. And that third option is how you use it with Cline. Now if you don't know about Cline pass, it is the 999 per month plan from the Claude team for open coding models. You get DeepSeek V 4.1 Flash, Kimi K 3 1 Pro, GLM 5.3, Qwen 38 Max, MiniMax M 31 Flash, and more with two to five times the normal rate limits. And Claude pass also works outside of Claude through the Claude API, which is OpenAI compatible. You just create an API key in the Claude dashboard. So here is the setup. In Claude, you pick the OpenAI compatible provider. For the base URL, you put localhost 8787/billy followed by the Claude API address. You paste your Claude API key, and for the model, you put Claude pass/deepseek V 4.1 Flash. Now every request from Claude goes through billion context, gets compressed, and then goes to Claude pass. The billion context repo lists Claude as a verified client for exactly this through the OpenAI compatible base URL. And this should work in Claude desktop as well. Claude desktop is the Claude agent as a standalone app, and it is really good for long tasks. You can run parallel sessions, you can schedule jobs, and you can import a Claude code or Codex conversation and continue it. And if you look at the provider list on the Claude desktop page, OpenAI compatible is right there next to Claude pass. So you use the same base URL, the same key, and the same model. Now you have a long flash session in a proper app where the context never blows up. That is a pretty great combo. Now why does this combo make sense? Claude pass gives you a flat price, but it still has a five hour window, a weekly limit, and a monthly limit. And a long session burns those limits by resending the history on every turn. Billion context cuts that history down, so the same plan lasts a lot longer. And DeepSeek V 4.1 Flash is the same model family that the benchmark was run on. Once it is running, you can open localhost 8787 in your browser. You get a dashboard, a list of your sessions, live logs, and a config editor. And if you type/acp cache in a supported client, it gives you a report with your cash hit rate, how many tokens each compression saved, and what broke the cash if it dropped. That is really useful for seeing whether it is actually saving you money. And if you want a GUI for orchestration, then Panda Code is what I use. Panda Code has an architect that holds the whole task and sends work to separate workers, and Cline is one of the harnesses in there. The architect is the session that lives the longest and grows the most, so that is where compression helps the most. And since workers can run on Pi, open code, or Kimi code, which all have native Billy plugins, you can keep the whole team lean. Now, I do have to mention the limitations. First, it is moving very fast. It is on version 0.121. It updates itself by default, and the master branch can be broken at any time, so install the release from NPM. Second, if you run it on your network with dash-host, there is no authentication at all, so only do that on a network you trust. Third, the Claude desktop apps code tab bypasses the proxy, so there you get no compression. Fourth, as we saw, exact recall drops, so if you need a verbatim line from far back, the model has to decompress it. And the docs are huge and very technical, so setup takes some reading. So to summarize, billion context is a proxy that lets the model compress its own history with tools in small ranges that can be restored while keeping the cash intact. The benchmarks on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash show a cheaper than full context, and on coding it was even slightly better. Put it in front of Cline Pass in Cline or Cline Desktop, and you get cheap open models plus sessions that just keep going. If your long agent sessions keep dying or costing too much, I would definitely give this a try. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking [music] the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.

items.title: Claude Code OS Setup: The $20 AI Coding OS
items.summary:
Bambooed is now Open-source & called PandaCode: https://github.com/aicodeking/pandacode
Join this channel to get access to perks:
https://www.youtube.com/channel/@aicodeking/join

In this video, I'll put together a complete AI coding setup on a Mac, starting with which Claude plan to buy and why Claude Pro at $20 a month is enough to begin. Then I'll prepare the Mac with Apple's Command Line Tools, Homebrew, Git, the GitHub CLI and Node 24 LTS, install Claude Code natively, and sign in with the subscription. After that, I'll add Zed as the editor with its external Claude Agent, show where T3 Code, Bambooed and Delta fit (including the subscription catch with Delta), and set up CLAUDE.md, Context7, the frontend-design and Superpowers plugins, and Claude in Chrome. Finally, I'll build and test a small reading-list app with plan mode and browser verification to show the daily workflow I'd actually use.

--
Key Takeaways:

💸 Claude's free plan doesn't include Claude Code; Pro at $20 a mont
items.author: AICodeKing
